strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: avoiding repeated LoRA fine-tuning across heterogeneous layer-wise quantization configurations for deployment-constrained models.

The proposed configuration-aware LoRA adjustment is compact and plausible: predicting an r-by-r adjustment per layer is a sensible way to reduce the output dimensionality compared with generating full LoRA parameters.
The paper includes a reasonably broad empirical study, covering RoBERTa-Large on GLUE, Qwen/LLaMA-family models on C4, multiple LoRA ranks, unseen configurations, and zero-shot downstream tasks.

The method often improves hypervolume and accuracy/perplexity tradeoffs relative to Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA, and Shared-LoRA, while using a single trained adjustment model rather than one adapter per configuration.
The motivation is clear, and the paper is generally readable, with useful appendices describing initialization, configuration selection, and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The main claims about arbitrary configuration adaptation are stronger than the evidence. The deployment-time selection procedure chooses configurations close to the optimized training set under a target bit budget, so the method is not fully demonstrated on arbitrary heterogeneous configurations far from the searched set.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. CoA-LoRA is evaluated over many configurations and optimized via configuration search, while Q-LoRA and LQ-LoRA are reported only at four bit-widths due to cost; the hypervolume comparison may therefore partly reflect denser sampling and configuration search rather than adapter quality alone.

Training-time accounting is underspecified and potentially favorable to the proposed method. It is unclear whether all costs of configuration evaluation, GP/EHVI search, integer programming initialization, calibration passes, and repeated candidate filtering are included consistently against baselines.

Important reproducibility details are missing or vague, including the architecture and size of the configuration-aware model, optimizer settings beyond learning rate, batch sizes, T1/T2 values, calibration/evaluation details for the GP, random seeds, and variance over runs.

The technical formulation of the finite-difference EHVI search over a high-dimensional discrete configuration space is not fully justified. Using continuous finite differences on configuration embeddings with delta=1 and only a small number of observed configurations may be brittle, but this is not analyzed.

Several ablations are incomplete. The paper studies search/no-search and rank, but does not isolate key components such as conditioning on layer name/block index, adjusting only L2 versus both LoRA factors, the number of training configurations, GP versus simpler search heuristics, or robustness to random configuration sets.

The reported gains are sometimes modest or inconsistent, especially in the C4 and zero-shot settings, and some baselines outperform CoA-LoRA on individual tasks. The paper would benefit from confidence intervals or multiple seeds to establish significance.
Algorithm 1 and parts of the appendix contain clarity issues and apparent pseudocode omissions, making the exact training/search loop difficult to reconstruct.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant practical problem: avoiding separate LoRA fine-tuning for many quantization configurations under heterogeneous deployment constraints.
The high-level idea of learning configuration-conditioned low-rank adapter adjustments is interesting and potentially useful if made technically and empirically convincing.
The paper includes experiments across GLUE tasks and several LLM backbones, plus some ablations on configuration search, rank, unseen configurations, and segmentation.
weaknesses: The technical presentation has serious unresolved issues. The finite-difference EHVI optimization is applied in a high-dimensional discrete configuration space via continuous embeddings, but the paper does not clearly define how perturbed embeddings are mapped back to valid quantization configurations. This makes the core search procedure difficult to assess or reproduce.

There are internal inconsistencies in the method and analysis. For example, Appendix C.1 appears to show high cross-bit similarity for L1 and very low similarity for L2, yet the text claims shared components are mostly in L2 and configuration-specific knowledge is in L1. This directly undermines the stated motivation for transforming L2.

The evaluation is not sufficiently fair or convincing. Q-LoRA and LQ-LoRA are evaluated only at four bit-widths, while CoA-LoRA is evaluated over many configurations and wider bit ranges; the hypervolume comparison can therefore favor the proposed method because of different curve coverage rather than genuinely better performance.

The claimed efficiency advantage is overstated. CoA-LoRA still requires nontrivial training plus configuration search, calibration evaluations, and integer-programming initialization, yet the paper repeatedly suggests no additional time cost or real-time adaptation without giving a complete accounting of all costs.

Important deployment claims are unsupported. The paper motivates edge deployment but does not report actual memory footprint, inference latency, adapter-generation overhead, energy, or hardware measurements on edge-like devices.

The baselines are incomplete for the stated contribution. Stronger mixed-precision quantization/search methods, adapter routing/hypernetwork baselines, and simpler interpolation or multi-task LoRA baselines are missing, making it hard to isolate whether the proposed configuration-aware model is the source of gains.

Reproducibility is weak. Key implementation details are underspecified, including GP kernel choices and hyperparameters, EHVI computation, projection/rounding of configurations, training data sizes, calibration batch construction, random seeds, variance over runs, and code availability.

Several reported results are modest or mixed despite strong claims. CoA-LoRA is not consistently better in accuracy gap across ranks/tasks, and the LLM perplexity table in the appendix shows cases where the proposed method is worse than alternatives depending on metric interpretation.

The hypervolume discussion is confusing and potentially inconsistent: the appendix says normalized objectives are constructed so smaller values are better, while the main text interprets larger HV as better. This raises concerns about metric definition and result interpretation.

The paper contains multiple clarity and rigor issues, including ambiguous notation, dimension/output descriptions that are hard to follow, unclear distinction between seen and unseen configurations, and conclusions that are stronger than the presented evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem: adapting LoRA fine-tuning to heterogeneous quantization configurations without retraining a separate adapter for each target budget.

The proposed CoA-LoRA mechanism is conceptually appealing: predicting small layer-wise r x r adjustment matrices is a reasonable way to make configuration-conditioned adaptation tractable, and the method is well motivated by the cost of one-adapter-per-configuration tuning.
The empirical evaluation is broader than many submissions in this area, covering GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large and C4/perplexity results on Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-2-7B.

Results are consistently positive against Q-LoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA, and Shared-LoRA, with meaningful improvements in hypervolume and generally favorable accuracy/perplexity gaps while reducing cumulative fine-tuning time.

The paper includes useful ablations on configuration search, rank sensitivity, unseen configurations, zero-shot downstream accuracy, and the number of Pareto segments, which supports the main empirical claims.
The central contribution has clear potential utility for deployment settings where many quantization budgets must be supported from one training procedure.
weaknesses: The claim of adapting to arbitrary quantization configurations is stronger than the evidence. The method is trained and selected around a finite searched set, and unseen-configuration evaluation appears to test nearby/interpolated configurations rather than genuinely arbitrary layer-wise configurations from the full combinatorial space.

The training-time comparison is somewhat favorable to the proposed method but not fully normalized. CoA-LoRA is compared against Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA evaluated at only four bit-widths, while the method itself uses configuration search, calibration evaluation, GP fitting, and integer programming; the accounting of all overheads and scaling with number of configurations is not completely transparent.

Several algorithmic details are underspecified or confusing, which affects reproducibility. For example, the finite-difference update is described over discrete configuration embeddings, the projection back to valid NF parameter choices is unclear, and the initial integer program in the appendix appears to have notation/dimensional inconsistencies.

The configuration search component may contribute substantially to gains, but the paper does not fully disentangle whether improvements come from better quantization configurations, the configuration-aware LoRA adjustment, or simply training over multiple carefully selected configurations.

The evaluation would be stronger with statistical variation across seeds, confidence intervals, and clearer reporting of absolute accuracy/perplexity values for all configurations rather than mainly hypervolume and averaged gaps.
The deployment motivation emphasizes edge devices, but there is little direct hardware evaluation: no latency, memory footprint, adapter-generation overhead, or on-device measurements are reported.

Some relevant baselines and variants are missing or only lightly discussed, especially quantization-aware LoRA methods beyond the selected comparisons, and it is unclear whether all baselines receive equally optimized quantization configurations.
Presentation has noticeable polish issues in equations, algorithm notation, and extracted figure text, which do not invalidate the work but make the technical procedure harder to verify.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practically important problem: adapting LoRA fine-tuning to many heterogeneous quantization configurations without training a separate adapter for every device or bit budget.

The proposed configuration-aware LoRA adjustment is a plausible and lightweight design: predicting an r x r layer-wise transformation is much more tractable than generating full LoRA parameters, and the parameter overhead is small.

The paper includes a reasonably broad empirical study across RoBERTa-Large on GLUE, Qwen2.5 models, LLaMA-2-7B, an additional LLaMA-2-13B result, multiple LoRA ranks, and both NF-style and integer mixed-precision quantization.

The results are promising: CoA-LoRA often improves hypervolume and average accuracy/perplexity relative to QLoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA, and Shared-LoRA, while requiring less training time than one-adapter-per-configuration baselines.
The ablations on configuration search, unseen configurations, rank sensitivity, and segment selection are useful and support the claim that the Pareto-based configuration set matters.
weaknesses: The main efficiency claim is not fully convincing. CoA-LoRA relies on configuration-specific SVD of the residual between full-precision and quantized weights, but the cost of computing these SVD-based LoRA factors for arbitrary deployment configurations is not clearly included in the reported training or adaptation time.

The comparison to baselines may be unfair for the hypervolume metric: CoA-LoRA is evaluated over many configurations, while expensive baselines are reported only at a few bit-widths. It is unclear how HV is computed under this mismatch and whether sparse baseline curves are penalized for evaluation budget rather than method quality.

There are methodological inconsistencies around the motivation for transforming L2. The text claims the adaptation signal is concentrated in L2, while Appendix C.1 appears to state that shared components are in L2 and configuration-specific knowledge is in L1; the displayed correlation values also seem difficult to reconcile with the written interpretation.

The optimization procedure is under-specified in important places: how discrete configurations are kept feasible after finite-difference updates, how categorical embeddings map back to valid bit/bucket choices, kernel and GP details, constraints during coordinate search, and exact evaluation/calibration protocols are not sufficiently clear.

The empirical evidence is promising but not yet decisive for a top-tier acceptance. There are no confidence intervals or multiple-seed results, and several reported gains are modest or mixed at individual bit-widths, especially on larger LLMs where CoA-LoRA is sometimes close to or worse than QLoRA/LQ-LoRA.

Important related baselines are missing or insufficiently discussed, including quantization-aware LoRA variants and recent sub-2/low-bit LoRA methods cited by the paper itself. This weakens the positioning of the contribution.

The paper overstates generality with phrases such as arbitrary configurations and no additional time cost. In practice, the method is evaluated within a specific discrete configuration space and appears to require configuration selection plus residual/SVD construction, so the deployment story is less clean than claimed.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the implementation link appears malformed or missing, some hyperparameters and search details are absent, and the dependence on solvers such as Gurobi for configuration initialization may limit reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant deployment problem: adapting LoRA-tuned quantized models across heterogeneous layer-wise quantization configurations without retraining a separate adapter for every setting.
The proposed configuration-conditioned low-rank adjustment is lightweight in parameter count and conceptually reasonable as a way to amortize adaptation across quantization choices.
The experiments cover several task/model settings, including GLUE with RoBERTa-Large and C4/perplexity experiments for Qwen and LLaMA models, plus some ablations on configuration search and rank.
weaknesses: The central empirical comparison is not convincing. CoA-LoRA is evaluated over many more configurations than the one-to-one baselines, while the hypervolume metric rewards broader coverage; this makes the reported HV gains difficult to interpret as algorithmic superiority rather than evaluation asymmetry.

The training-time claims are under-supported and potentially misleading. The paper claims no additional time cost, but CoA-LoRA trains over a configuration set and performs GP/Pareto search and configuration evaluations; it is unclear whether all search, calibration, SVD initialization, and configuration-selection costs are included fairly against baselines.

The baselines appear weakly or unfairly treated. QLoRA/LQ-LoRA are only run on a small set of bit-widths, while CoA-LoRA is optimized for a large configuration set; there is no strong amortized baseline such as interpolation/conditioning without Pareto search, multi-task LoRA with matched configuration exposure, or a shared adapter trained with comparable compute and configuration sampling.

The method description has internal inconsistencies and unclear technical details. The paper motivates transforming one LoRA factor using similarity observations, but the appendix text appears to state that configuration-specific information is primarily in the other factor. The finite-difference update over discrete configurations is also underspecified and does not clearly ensure valid configurations after each step.

The claim of adaptation to arbitrary quantization configurations is overstated. At inference the method appears to select configurations close to the learned/filtered set, and the unseen-configuration study is limited; it does not establish robust generalization over the enormous discrete configuration space.

The evaluation does not adequately support the edge-device motivation. There are no real memory, latency, throughput, energy, or hardware heterogeneity measurements, only average bit-width and task metrics.

Several results are unstable or mixed despite strong claims. CoA-LoRA is not consistently better than QLoRA/LQ-LoRA across all individual bit-widths, ranks, and tasks, yet the paper repeatedly presents the method as broadly superior.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier submission: the implementation link is missing/incomplete, solver dependence is mentioned, many hyperparameters and compute details are sparse, and statistical variation or multiple seeds are not reported.
Writing and presentation contain noticeable issues, including incomplete text, confusing metric descriptions, crowded plots, and claims that are stronger than the provided evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: adapting LoRA-tuned quantized models across many heterogeneous quantization configurations without training a separate adapter for each configuration.

The proposed CoA-LoRA formulation is technically plausible and well motivated: generating compact r x r configuration-conditioned adjustments is a sensible way to reduce the hypernetwork output space while retaining layer-specific adaptation.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Large, C4 perplexity with Qwen/LLaMA-scale models, integer mixed-precision quantization, different LoRA ranks, unseen configurations, and a 13B model appendix experiment.

Empirical results are consistently favorable: CoA-LoRA often improves hypervolume and accuracy/perplexity tradeoffs over QLoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA, and Shared-LoRA, while avoiding per-configuration fine-tuning.

The paper includes useful ablations for configuration search, random extension, segment count, rank sensitivity, and seen versus unseen configurations, which strengthens the case that both the conditional mapper and the Pareto-based configuration search matter.
weaknesses: Some central claims are stronger than the evidence. The method is said to support arbitrary configurations with no additional time cost, but configuration selection still depends on a searched configuration set, constrained bit budgets, Gurobi-style optimization, and proximity to training configurations; the experiments mostly test nearby or curated configurations rather than truly arbitrary deployment settings.

The time comparison is not fully convincing. QLoRA and LQ-LoRA are evaluated as repeated one-to-one fine-tuning over several configurations, whereas CoA-LoRA trains one conditional model and performs configuration search. The accounting of search, calibration evaluation, GP updates, SVD initialization, and solver cost is not sufficiently detailed for a clean efficiency conclusion.

The hypervolume comparison may favor CoA-LoRA because it is evaluated over many more configurations than the one-to-one baselines, which are only run at a small set of bit-widths due to cost. The paper should clarify interpolation/curve construction and ensure the HV metric is comparable across methods with different sampling densities.

The motivation for transforming only one LoRA factor is somewhat confusing. The main text states adaptation signal is concentrated in L2, while Appendix C.1 appears to describe shared versus configuration-specific structure in a way that is not fully aligned with the chosen parameterization. This weakens the mechanistic justification.

The method description has several underspecified implementation details, including the exact kernel/input representation for the GP in the high-dimensional discrete space, how invalid finite-difference steps are handled, how f1 is evaluated efficiently during search, and whether calibration data leakage or overfitting to task validation-like signals is avoided.

Reproducibility is weaker than ideal for a top-tier paper: the implementation link appears incomplete in the manuscript, and key hyperparameters/search costs/code-level details are scattered or omitted. The dependence on Gurobi may also complicate reproduction.

The evaluation would be stronger with statistical variation across seeds and a more direct comparison to conditional LoRA/hypernetwork adapter generation methods adapted to quantized settings, even if those methods require modifications.
The paper has presentation issues, including malformed extracted text in figures, an incomplete sentence about implementation availability, and occasional overclaiming in the conclusion.
